Two forward references in g2_s2 point to the wrong section, same off-by-one as §0. Line 196 (Gotcha after the linearity recipe): 'It is not a licence to write $\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]$ (false in general; true under independence, §5)' — independence of random variables is §4.5 and $\mathbb{E}[XY]$ under independence is §4.6, not §5. Line 249 (marksman part d): 'write $X = X_1+\cdots+X_{10}$ with $X_i$ the indicator of a hit on shot $i$; that is §5 machinery' — the indicator derivation of the binomial mean and variance is §4.8. Both should read §4.

Factually false software claim in the §1.5 Gotcha 'geometric random variables start at 1, and the convention varies' (line 335): 'Many texts and software packages (including scipy.stats.geom vs. numpy.random.geometric conventions) instead count failures before the first success, giving $Y = X - 1$ with $p_Y(k) = (1-p)^k p$.' Verified by running both: scipy.stats.geom.pmf(1, 0.3) = 0.3 and geom.pmf(0, 0.3) = 0.0 (support starts at 1), and numpy's rng.geometric(0.3, 10000) has min 1 and sample mean 3.31 ≈ 1/p. The two libraries AGREE on the trials-counting (k ≥ 1) convention; neither uses the failures-before-success convention. The underlying mathematical point (the two conventions differ by 1, means 1/p vs (1-p)/p) is correct — only the cited example is wrong. Correct = drop the scipy/numpy parenthetical, or replace it with a genuine example of the shifted convention (e.g. scipy.stats.nbinom(1, p), or the 'number of failures' convention used in many texts).

Practice 2.10 solution displays incorrect arithmetic: 'var(Y) = E[Y](E[X]-E[Y]) = 37 × 2.28 = 84.5'. 37 × 2.28 = 84.36, not 84.5; the true value 84.5 = 169/2 (key bus_varY) needs the unrounded gap 2.283784 (37 × 2.283784 = 84.5). Correct = write '37 × 2.2838 = 84.5' or '37 × (39.28 − 37) ≈ 84.4, exactly 169/2 = 84.5 with the unrounded means'.

§2.2, final justification of the expected-value-rule derivation (line 99): 'the double sum is a re-bracketing of a single sum, and re-bracketing a sum of nonnegative terms does not change it.' The terms are $g(x)p_X(x)$, which are NOT nonnegative in general — Example 2.2 immediately below uses $X$ uniform on $\{-2,\ldots,2\}$, and §2.4 uses $Y = 2X-3$ with negative values. The correct condition is absolute convergence, $\sum_x |g(x)|p_X(x) < \infty$ — which is exactly the well-definedness hypothesis already stated on line 14. Correct = 'the terms $g(x)p_X(x)$ are absolutely summable by the standing hypothesis of line 14, so regrouping does not change the sum' (or note that the masses are nonnegative and the rearrangement is of a finite sum when the range is finite).

§2.1, line 14: 'the weights $p_X(x)$ sum to 1, so $\mathbb{E}[X]$ is a weighted average of the possible values: it always lies between the smallest and the largest value $X$ can take.' False as stated for a countably infinite range with no largest value — and §2.6 of this same section is built on exactly such a variable (the St. Petersburg payout $W$, whose values $2^k$ are unbounded and whose mean is infinite). Correct = restrict the claim to bounded/finite ranges, e.g. 'when $X$ takes finitely many values, $\mathbb{E}[X]$ lies between the smallest and the largest of them'.

§2.4(a), line 233: 'The peak is at $k=2$, next to the mean $\mathbb{E}[X]=2$ computed in (d).' The peak and the mean are at the same point ($k=2$, $np = 2$), not adjacent. Correct = 'The peak is at $k=2$, which here coincides with the mean $\mathbb{E}[X]=np=2$'.

THE HAT PROBLEM (L07 slides 7 and 8) IS NEVER SOLVED ANYWHERE IN THE NOTE. The L05/L06/L07 inventory lists 8 [UNSOLVED EXAMPLE] blanks plus 2 [DERIVATION GAP]s for it: P(X_i=1)=1/n, E[X_i]=1/n, 'Are the X_i independent?', E[X]=1 (slide 7); E[X_i^2]=1/n, P(X_1X_2=1)=P(X_1=1)P(X_2=1|X_1=1)=(1/n)(1/(n-1)), E[X^2]=2, Var(X)=1 (slide 8). Grep of all six g2 fragments finds only three passing mentions and zero derivation: (a) g2_s4.html line ~812, a forward promise inside Example 4.8 ('precisely why the same argument will solve the hat problem, where the X_i are dependent') that is never redeemed; (b) g2_s5.html line ~178, an Interpretation box asserting 'computing var(X)=1 in that same problem took a whole extra slide of work with the cross terms E[X_iX_j]' — the work itself is absent; (c) g2_s5.html line ~201, one cheat-sheet table row stating '1 and 1'. Compounding this, g2_s4's srcref explicitly scopes itself to 'L07 slides 1-6', so slides 7-8 are orphaned by construction, while g2_s0 line 48 and computes/g2_s0_figs.py line 119 both PROMISE the hat problem to the reader. Fix: add a full '.ex' box (e.g. Example 4.9, or a new h3 '4.9 The hat problem') in g2_s4.html immediately after §4.8, deriving every blank step by step — P(X_i=1)=1/n by symmetry of a uniformly random permutation; E[X_i]=1/n; the X_i are dependent (P(X_2=1|X_1=1)=1/(n-1) != 1/n) yet E[X]=n*(1/n)=1 by linearity alone; then X_i^2=X_i so E[X_i^2]=1/n; E[X_iX_j]=P(X_i=1,X_j=1)=(1/n)(1/(n-1)) for the n(n-1) ordered off-diagonal pairs; E[X^2]=n*(1/n)+n(n-1)*1/(n(n-1))=1+1=2; var(X)=2-1=1 — plus 1-3 practice questions. Extend g2_s4's srcref to 'L07 slides 1-8', and add a numeric cross-check (n=3,5,10,100) to computes/g2_s4.py.
